articles.title: Men face new pressure to stay ‘hot’ as they age — and it’s not just about living longer
articles.summary: Plastic surgeon Dr. Krishna Vyas reveals why men no longer feel stigma around cosmetic procedures and shares the foundational steps for extending 'hotspan'.
articles.body: Maintaining healthy cholesterol and blood pressure, along with regular physical activity, are widely recommended components of healthy aging. But as interest in longevity grows, some older adults are looking beyond extending their healthspan — the number of years lived free of disease — to prioritize looking, feeling and remaining physically attractive as they age. Experts say the desire to maintain one’s appearance — the pursuit of "hotness" — can be psychological, shaped in part by a disconnect between how people feel and the changes they see in the mirror. COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY "It really isn't about age," Dr. Krishna Vyas, M.D., Ph.D., a plastic surgeon at Fleckman Plastic Surgery on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan, told Fox News Digital. "I think it's when you look in the mirror and you're like, 'I don't recognize myself. I don't recognize the way I feel. I don't identify with how my appearance isn't concordant with how I feel at that point.'" Men now account for roughly 15% of all cosmetic procedures, according to data from the American Society of Plastic Surgeons. Social barriers that may have previously prevented men from seeking aesthetic treatment have diminished in the last two decades, Vyas noted. "In the past, there was a stigma ... men were once shamed or ashamed of seeking out things that improve their appearance, especially in aesthetics, but that barrier has fallen significantly," he said. DO RED LIGHT THERAPY AND COLD PLUNGES REALLY WORK? A DOCTOR REVEALS THE TRUTH The motivations driving men to pursue "looksmaxxing" — a social media term for enhanced efforts to improve physical appearance — range from maintaining a competitive edge in youth-centric workplaces to addressing subtle signs of aging, such as dark under-eye circles or loss of jawline definition, according to Vyas. Treatments range from minimally invasive procedures like Botox and laser therapy, to surgical interventions like chest masculinization and liposuction. "The misconception often is that minimally invasive treatments will fix things and have no side effects," Vyas cautioned, noting that improper or excessive non-surgical treatments can change the normal layers and contours of facial tissue. 5 steps to looking your best Before jumping to aesthetic procedures as quick-fix substitutes for biological health, the surgeon recommends taking the following steps to improve physical appearance. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES No. 1: Eliminate nicotine Complete abstinence from all forms of nicotine is essential to maintaining microvascular circulation and preventing premature skin breakdown, according to Vyas. No. 2: Stick to your skincare Avoid over-hyped trends and multi-step routines, the experts recommended. Guidelines from the American Academy of Dermatology point to two daily essentials: a morning broad-spectrum sunscreen to block photoaging UV rays, and a topical retinoid at night to stimulate cell turnover. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER No. 3: Manage weight Maintaining a healthy weight can prevent the chronic, systemic inflammation that is linked to metabolic syndrome, which directly accelerates structural skin and tissue aging. No. 4: Address hair loss early Intervene early at the first sign of thinning. Evidence-based medical treatments, like FDA-approved finasteride and minoxidil, remain the primary standard for maintaining hair density before follicle loss becomes permanent. No. 5: Stay active "The real longevity drug is exercise — aerobic and non-aerobic strength training exercises," Vyas said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Someone who's looking for a hotspan or a healthspan, because they're so intimately related … I think they should focus on the basics to start ... the foundation is what's most important," the surgeon added.

articles.title: How easy is it to find an NHS dentist? It depends on where you live
articles.summary: Nearly 600 practices in England have withdrawn from NHS dentistry over the last 10 years, as the service heads towards a two-tier system.
articles.body:
Hundreds of dentist practices are abandoning NHS work as the service drifts towards a two-tier system, new analysis suggests.

Data analysed by the Nuffield Trust found that nearly 600 practices in England have withdrawn from NHS dentistry over the last 10 years. The decline has been particularly sharp in parts of the South West and East of England, raising concerns about growing inequalities in access to care.

The analysis suggests more than one in 10 dental practices that once offered NHS care no longer do so, leaving it near impossible for some communities to find NHS appointments.

NHS dental activity is 8% lower than it was pre Covid, while six in 10 adults have not seen an NHS dentist in two years. Of those who attempted to get a new appointment in the last two years, just 38% were successful, according to the NHS GP Patient Survey.

Cornwall, Devon and Northamptonshire have seen some of the biggest reductions in the number of practices offering NHS care. In Cornwall, more than a quarter of practices that previously offered NHS treatment have stopped doing so, making it one of the starkest examples of the shift away from NHS dentistry.

The findings come as ministers have pledged to tackle so-called "dental deserts", but dentists say the current deal is not viable. Many have handed back their NHS contracts because to work is loss-making.

In Somerset, fewer than one in five dental practices now offers NHS services. Alan, 83, who lives in the county, says he has given up trying to find an NHS dentist.

"I used to try, but getting a dental appointment anywhere near where I live would be impossible," he says.

Alan has only one tooth remaining after the others "crumbled out over the years" and says he has had to adapt what he eats, although he jokes that he has perfected a way of eating Brazil nuts.

Vivak Shah, who runs three dental practices in Northamptonshire, continues to offer NHS treatment but says it operates at a loss. He no longer takes on new NHS patients.

"Each year we struggle to decide what to do, and there is a limit to how much the private side can cover the NHS losses," says Shah.

He warned that if practices stop providing NHS treatment, many patients could be left in pain or forced to seek help elsewhere in the health service, including hospital accident and emergency departments.

"A contract handed back in one town attracts little national attention on its own but repeated across the country for a decade it amounts to the quiet transformation of dentistry into a two-tier service," says Mark Dayan, head of public affairs at the Nuffield Trust.

"Access to dental care increasingly depends on what people can afford to pay and where they live."

Jim Sykes is a dentist in Hexham. He handed back his NHS contract in 2024.

"It was a really hard emotional decision, but the NHS work was running at such a loss. I had to think of my team of staff and make it work," he says. Sykes asked if he could continue treating just children but was told he had to accept adults as well, or give up the NHS work.

"There has been a real breakdown in trust for me. Even if there was a new government offer, I would still be very nervous about entering a new NHS contract," he says.

Sykes says that none of his friends in his graduating class in dentistry still works in the NHS. "My friends have gone private, retired or teach - any pathway to avoid NHS dentistry."

Shiv Pabary, chair of the British Dental Association's General Dental Practice Committee, says the situation is "the direct result of choices made by successive governments". He warns that unless ministers "fix and fund NHS dentistry", more dentists could choose to reduce their NHS work or leave the service altogether.

Overall dentist practice numbers have risen in England over the last decade.

"This is not a shortage of dentistry but a shortage of NHS dentistry," says Dayan. "Practices will need to be incentivised back into NHS work in the places where the NHS footprint has thinned most."

While most parts of England recorded declines in practices offering NHS dental care, the reductions were smallest in North West London, the Black Country and North East London.

North East London was the only area to see any increase during the period, recording one additional practice offering NHS treatment compared with a decade ago.

Every other region of England saw the number of NHS dental practices fall.

Looking at the number of practices doing NHS work is not the same as looking at exactly how much health service capacity there is - practices can vary in size. But if you look at other measures such as the amount of treatment being done, the numbers are still down, although not as steep as the fall in practice numbers.

The government says that it is changing the dental contract and training more dentists in the areas most in need. The government says it will also make it a requirement for newly qualified dentists to practice in the NHS for a minimum period of at least three years.

Campaign group 38 degrees calls the current dental crisis "shameful", with people being "forced to pay money they can't afford or suffer with the pain, shame, and further complications that come from being denied vital NHS healthcare".

Have you been able to find an NHS dentist in your area? Tell us your story.

articles.title: Doctors wrongly said I was too young to have endometriosis at 13
articles.summary: Grace, 14, feels doctors were dismissive of her pain. She wants others to know the symptoms.
articles.body:
Every month, at about the time of her period, Grace has to be taken to hospital.

She is often in so much pain her parents have to carry her to the car. She can wait hours to be seen in A&E, only to be sent home in tears with more strong painkillers.

For a long time, Grace - who's now 14 and is from Yorkshire - felt doctors were dismissive of her pain. "I feel like I was seen as a girl who didn't want to go to school and was being dramatic," she says.

She was given multiple possible reasons for her symptoms: irritable bowel syndrome, a cyst, anxiety and "just a bad period". But, she says, "I knew it was more than that."

Doctors told her time and again that it could not be endometriosis - an incurable condition causing lesions and scarring on internal organs and around the body , external - because she was too young. Grace says her requests for further investigation were ignored.

'It's like heated barbed wire around my abdomen'

Grace's periods began when she was 11, and by 13, she was having excruciating pains around the time of menstruation. She describes it as if "heated barbed wire" were wrapped around her abdomen: "It's like my organs are being pulled apart."

She is often bedbound and, whenever she has exhausted the painkillers she has at home, she has to go in to hospital, where she is regularly given morphine. She has also been given co-codamol and tramadol.

Dependency on strong drugs like opioids worries her. "It's scary," she says, "because I don't want to have to rely on them for the rest of my life."

But the most frustrating thing for Grace, and why she contacted BBC Your Voice, is because she does not feel medical experts recognise that teenagers and adolescents can suffer from endometriosis.

Grace's GP did not diagnose her condition and nor did the first consultant she saw privately.

She says: "Even a specialist didn't believe me. And if a specialist won't listen to me, who will?" It was not until the family pushed for a second private opinion that she got a positive diagnosis.

Endometriosis, which occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows outside it, can cause debilitating symptoms, such as pelvic pain, heavy periods and fatigue. About 10% of women are affected by it, according to NHS data.

This week BBC presenter Emma Barnett revealed she had to have a hysterectomy for her endometriosis - which she said she never wanted to have.

It can develop at any age once periods begin - and it is a common misconception that only older women suffer from the condition, says the charity Endometriosis UK,

Faye Farthing, a spokesperson for the charity, says the government, NHS and health practitioners need to improve menstrual health education for young people "if we are to ensure the next generation are not robbed of the future they deserve".

The charity says it can take a long time to diagnose endometriosis - an average of nine years in older women.

And in the early stages, for example with teenagers, it often doesn't show up on an ultrasound scan. However, new tests are being developed which will help spot the condition earlier.

Getting pregnant can be more difficult - even aged 14, Grace says she has been warned it is likely to affect her fertility. She's been advised she may not be able to have children after the age of 30 because of damage to her reproductive organs.

She feels rushed: "I have to have kids within the next 15 years, otherwise I might not be able to."

Paediatric gynaecologist Dr Gail Busby says nearly 80% of adolescents will have painful periods, but clinicians should recognise when a patient's symptoms are not normal - like missing school, missing PE every month or not going out with friends.

She says: "When you're in bed and your best friend is a hot water bottle - that's not normal."

Grace's case, showing symptoms at the age of 13, is not unusual, says Dr Busby, who sees girls both younger and older than Grace at her clinics. As well as her NHS work, she has opened a private adolescent endometriosis clinic in Manchester.

The impact of symptoms is not just physical. Girls like Grace are more likely to suffer with anxiety or depression because their pain affects what is an important time for educational, emotional and social development.

"We should enjoy adolescence," Dr Busby says, "but they can't do what they enjoy doing, what their peers are enjoying doing."

There is a history of endometriosis in Grace's family, but her mum Samantha says that did not make it any easier to get a diagnosis.

"When your child's on the floor in pain, it's very clear it's not just a bad period. But professionals say 'Oh we'll just put you on the pill for six months and see see how we go.'"

Grace has recently had a laparoscopy - keyhole surgery - to remove her endometriosis.

She hopes the procedure will help relieve her symptoms, at least temporarily. She has been advised to take a hormonal contraceptive to help slow monthly tissue growth and lessen the pain.

By speaking out, Grace hopes more teenagers will have the confidence to pursue a diagnosis. "I felt I was going crazy. That it was all in my head," she says. "But actually, you know your body best and your pain is real."

Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Get in touch.

The impact of symptoms is not just physical. Girls like Grace are more likely to suffer with anxiety or depression because their pain affects what is an important time for educational, emotional and social development.
"We should enjoy adolescence," Dr Busby says, "but they can't do what they enjoy doing, what their peers are enjoying doing."
There is a history of endometriosis in Grace's family, but her mum Samantha says that did not make it any easier to get a diagnosis.
"When your child's on the floor in pain, it's very clear it's not just a bad period. But professionals say 'Oh we'll just put you on the pill for six months and see see how we go.'"
Grace has recently had a laparoscopy - keyhole surgery - to remove her endometriosis.
She hopes the procedure will help relieve her symptoms, at least temporarily. She has been advised to take a hormonal contraceptive to help slow monthly tissue growth and lessen the pain.

By speaking out, Grace hopes more teenagers will have the confidence to pursue a diagnosis. "I felt I was going crazy. That it was all in my head," she says. "But actually, you know your body best and your pain is real."
Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Get in touch.

articles.title: Louisiana girl, 8, dies after contracting suspected brain-eating amoeba linked to lake swim
articles.summary: Lillian Smart's family says the 8-year-old's brain injuries were too severe to survive after contracting Naegleria fowleri while swimming in a lake.
articles.body: Lillian Smart, an 8-year-old girl who health officials believe contracted a brain-eating amoeba while swimming in a northern Louisiana lake, died Saturday at a Ruston hospital from an infection linked to the pathogen. Lillian died one day after celebrating her eighth birthday. "The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from," the Smart family said in a statement posted Sunday morning on Facebook. "Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?" The Louisiana Department of Health announced Wednesday that a state resident had been hospitalized after becoming infected with Naegleria fowleri, a microscopic amoeba that can cause a rare and often deadly brain infection. MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000 State health officials have not publicly identified Lillian as the patient referenced in the announcement. Her family, however, said on social media that she had been admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit at a Ruston hospital and identified Naegleria fowleri as the cause of her illness. The health department said the infection in the case it announced was most likely acquired while the patient was swimming in Lake Claiborne shortly before becoming ill. A representative for the Louisiana Department of Health did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Louisiana Department of Health records identify three previous deaths associated with Naegleria fowleri in the state since 2011. BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE Two happened in 2011. A 20-year-old man in St. Bernard Parish died after using tap water to rinse his sinuses, while a 51-year-old woman in DeSoto Parish died after using tap water for a similar purpose. In 2013, a 4-year-old boy contracted the amoeba while visiting a home in St. Bernard Parish, where he had played on a slip-and-slide. State officials later reported that CDC testing detected Naegleria fowleri in the parish water system. Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, or PAM, an extremely rare brain infection that can develop when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain. People cannot become infected by swallowing contaminated water. The amoeba is not found in saltwater or properly chlorinated swimming pools. DEADLY BACTERIA FOUND IN WATERS NEAR LUXURY VACATION DESTINATION AHEAD OF SUMMER Symptoms typically begin with headache, fever, nausea and vomiting before progressing to a stiff neck, seizures and coma. Symptoms generally appear about five days after infection, and the disease can lead to death within about one to two weeks. About 97% of people who develop PAM die from the infection, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The CDC reported two PAM cases nationwide last year. Of the 173 infections documented over roughly the past 90 years, nearly 91% occurred in July and August.

articles.title: Four ways to make sure your will protects your family and avoids added grief
articles.summary: An estate planning attorney can ensure your will meets state-specific requirements, but making it findable is just as critical for your loved ones.
articles.body: There is no worse feeling in life than when a loved one passes away. And when that individual has not communicated his or her wishes or shared key information, that can add an additional burden of time, money and stress to loved ones’ grief. As August is National Make a Will Month, here are four suggestions to help you make sure you have your will made and updated in a manner that will help your loved ones sort through your estate and continue your legacy in the best manner possible. Make your will today! CEO’S FIRE DEATH SPARKS MYSTERY, WILL FIGHT OVER TECH TITAN'S FORTUNE When it comes to estate planning, having a will is important. Having one that is done properly is more important. There are online services that can help you, but I recommend meeting with a local estate planning attorney. Not only will a professional make sure that your wishes are accounted for properly, but they will understand state-specific requirements and regulations. Moreover, many estate planning attorneys can help with more than just the legal aspects of estate planning; they can also help or find you someone to help with tax planning and any related entities, such as trusts, to make sure your assets are passed down in the most tax-efficient manner. Explore making gifts and other plans now RICKY GERVAIS JOKES UK INHERITANCE TAX MAY FINALLY PUSH HIM TO MARRY LONGTIME PARTNER AFTER 40 YEARS As you meet with an estate planning professional or your accountant, you can explore making gifts to loved ones today. This may bring you more satisfaction, so that you can see your loved ones benefit from what you plan to leave them instead of waiting until you are gone. In 2026, you can gift $19,000 individually ($38,000 for married couples) per person, tax free for the year. Again, consult a professional for assistance to make sure you are crossing all your "t’s" and dotting your "is" regarding any gifting. Also, if you have family members who can handle the discussion, dividing up possessions, whether passed now or later, as a family can help minimize fighting among family members down the road. Moreover, many in the younger generations aren’t interested in the same physical mementos as those who are older. If you have a china set or a collection of statues that hasn’t been used in years, and nobody in the family wants them, you can explore making plans for disposal now – whether that means selling or donating the items. This can generate extra cash, tax deductions or even find a home with someone who you know will enjoy them. As a bonus, it will create less "cleanup" down the road for loved ones. Make your will findable MAN ACCUSED OF STEALING MORE THAN $735K AS POWER OF ATTORNEY TO PURCHASE PROPERTY, ONLYFANS AND LIFE COACHING One of the biggest issues I have seen with those who have wills is that their loved ones can’t find it (or don’t know which is the most recent copy). Preparing your wishes and information but not making them accessible to your loved ones defeats the purpose. Put your will, along with other key information (like a listing of your financial accounts and advisors or a key to your safe deposit box) and any personal wishes in a legacy and wishes planning kit. You can use one like the kit I created after my father’s passing, Future File, or you can make your own if you prefer. As you meet with an estate planning professional or your accountant, you can explore making gifts to loved ones today. This may bring you more satisfaction, so that you can see your loved ones benefit from what you plan to leave them instead of waiting until you are gone. Whichever route you go, make sure your family members either have access to your kit and its contents now or know how to access it and can do so in case of an emergency or if you pass. Review your will regularly OLIVER TREE MADE EERIE COMMENTS ABOUT HIS WILL WEEKS BEFORE FATAL HELICOPTER CRASH IN RIO DE JANEIRO A friend of mine’s mother was gravely ill and told my friend about her will. When my friend had an estate planning attorney review it, it turned out that it did not reflect what her mother’s current wishes were; rather, it contained some changes other family members had suggested many years ago that her mother had forgotten about. If this hadn’t been reviewed, her mother would not have left her assets to her grandchildren, but rather to distant cousins. That underscores why it is important to review your will regularly and make any updates if circumstances change over the years. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Additionally, if you have financial accounts, retirement plans or policies, such as insurance policies, that have beneficiaries, make sure that those are up to date, accurate and match your wishes. Beneficiary designations supersede wills, and so beneficiaries will receive the payments, even if they differ from your will. Check this on a regular basis as you review and update your will. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Saving your loved ones dozens of hours of time, giving them peace of mind and reducing uncertainty and even infighting during a very difficult time are the best things that you can leave behind as part of your legacy. That only happens with the proper planning today. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM CAROL ROTH

articles.title: 'Perfect' workout formula can take just 10 minutes a day, Hilaria Baldwin says
articles.summary: Hilaria Baldwin shares her "perfect" workout trifecta of cardio, strength training and stretching, plus tips for building exercise consistency.
articles.body: Being motivated to work out is one thing, but staying committed to a routine is what yields results, experts say. In an interview with Fox News Digital, certified yoga and fitness instructor Hilaria Baldwin shared her tips for building an effective exercise routine – and sticking to it. "One of the most important things about exercise is consistency," said the mother of seven. "For many of us, life gets in the way – we are parents and we work and all the chaos comes in, so bite-sized movements are really important." CHIEFS HEIRESS GRACIE HUNT REVEALS WHY SHE LIFTS HEAVY WEIGHTS — AND DOESN’T COUNT CALORIES Baldwin revealed that her "perfect" workout routine trifecta always includes cardio, strength training and stretching, even if it’s just 10 minutes per day. For lasting consistency, a fitness routine should fit naturally into one’s lifestyle and schedule, Baldwin said. She recommends setting aside kid-free, work-free blocks of time for movement and self-care. Baldwin said she makes time for a daily run as her cardio, which she said helps "work out her lungs." She also incorporates stretching and strength training, which might include physically picking up her kids or toning with weights. She has also started exercising with her children as a way to blend family time with physical activity. DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE The instructor emphasized consistency without overcommitment, noting that doing too much, too soon can lead to burnout. "If something's overwhelming, we're not going to do it," Baldwin said. "Ultimately, we are going to be creatures of habit … we are going do what we feel like needs to get done – but starting to think of a workout more like brushing our teeth is really important." "People are not moving their bodies enough and then we get sick," she went on. "So, the question is, can we do a little bit to prevent that? And obviously not everything can be prevented, but we know that we should move our bodies most days." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Baldwin advised against "biting off more than you can chew." For example, instead of running three miles as a response to being frustrated about your fitness goals, try running for just 10 minutes – or run for just two minutes at a time and take walking breaks. "Doing something is better than thinking about it and doing nothing," she added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The fitness instructor also suggested making exercise a family commitment, helping to reinforce that movement and self-care are priorities. "As moms, we [often] put ourselves last," she said. "Everybody says put your oxygen mask on first, but we don't do that." "I think showing our children that we are human and we are worth taking care of is really important – not just for our relationship with them, but how they will treat themselves when they're older." When life gets busy, she said, it’s easy to make excuses for not working out. Baldwin admitted that on most days, especially in the summer heat, she has "zero interest" in going for a run. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "But I know that I'm not going to regret it," she said. "It’s just about creating the habit and saying, ‘Okay, I'm going to do this, and it's going to be 30 minutes, and I might hate it, but I’m going to be happy to do it.’" Baldwin added, "Showing up is the hardest thing. Once you do it and you create a commitment, it completely changes everything." 'Love yourself' Baldwin encouraged the public, especially women, to tap into how "special and unique each person’s body is." "Start loving yourself and loving your body, no matter what outside opinions you feel like people are directing at you," she said. "Feel capable and feel strong and that you're worth investing in." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Baldwin shared that she herself has struggled "tremendously" with this in her own life. "That is one of the reasons that I show up – to tell my body, ‘I love you, you're worth it.’" She continued, "Nobody has ever existed who is exactly like you, and no one will ever be exactly like you again. So please live every single day cherishing your body, your unique self, and let's have fun and move together."

articles.title: Anti-aging supplements taken by millions may undermine cancer treatment, study warns
articles.summary: Popular NAD+-boosting supplements like NMN and nicotinamide riboside may shield pancreatic cancer cells from chemotherapy, a new study warns.
articles.body: Over-the-counter anti-aging supplements taken by millions of Americans to boost energy and lessen the side effects of chemotherapy may actually impair cancer treatments, a new study suggests. Researchers at the Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine found that popular vitamin B3 derivatives – including nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide (NAM) – could help cancer cells survive chemotherapy. Those compounds are used by the body to produce NAD+, a molecule that helps cells generate energy and repair damage. IV THERAPY AND SUPPLEMENTS UNDER SCRUTINY AS EXPERTS WARN OF POTENTIAL SIDE EFFECTS The study, published in the journal Cancer Letters, examined how these supplements interact with treatments for pancreatic cancer, a particularly deadly form of the disease with a 13% five-year survival rate, according to the American Cancer Society. While boosting NAD+ levels through dietary supplements can offer health benefits to non-cancerous cells, pancreatic cancer cells may exploit the extra resources to repair damage caused by chemotherapy and avoid cell death, the researchers found. In both laboratory settings and animal models, the supplements shielded cancer cells against three common chemotherapy drugs: oxaliplatin, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine. As a result, tumors survived chemotherapy doses that typically would prove fatal to them. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Our findings highlight a potentially concerning role for NAD+-boosting supplements in the context of active cancer, especially when used in conjunction with chemotherapy," said study lead Jordan Winter, a professor at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine and co-leader of the developmental therapeutics program at the Case Comprehensive Cancer Center, in the press release. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Our discovery is a call to action for the medical community." The study notes that these B3 derivatives are not considered dangerous for healthy individuals using them for general wellness. However, the risk becomes significant for patients currently undergoing active cancer therapy. "This research is a critical reminder that ‘natural’ doesn’t always mean safe, especially in the complex biology of cancer treatment," Winter added. In light of the findings, the research team recommends that oncology teams begin routinely screening patients for supplement use. They also called for more studies into how NAD+ precursors interact with cancer therapies. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Winter urged patients currently in treatment to consult their oncologists before taking any over-the-counter supplements. Because the study relied on laboratory cell cultures and animal models, the findings may not directly translate to how human patients process these supplements during treatment, the team noted. Additionally, the research focused exclusively on pancreatic cancer, meaning the supplements may not have the same effect on chemotherapy for other cancer types or with different drug combinations. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The study also only evaluated short-term cellular responses under controlled laboratory conditions and not human clinical trials, so it remains unclear how these supplements could affect cancer patients over time. Fox News Digital reached out to multiple NAD+ supplement manufacturers for comment.

articles.title: HPV home-testing kits now available for women who have missed cervical screening
articles.summary: Nearly four million women in England can order a self-testing kits to check for high-risk HPV.
articles.body:
Women who have missed a cervical screening appointment in England are to be offered HPV self-testing kits by the NHS.

Over the next year, nearly four million will receive invites on the NHS App or via text message, email or letter to order a free kit to use at home.

Figures show around a third of women who are eligible cervical cancer screening have not taken up the offer recently.

The self-testing kits are designed to get more women checked for high-risk HPV virus, which causes nearly all cases of cervical cancer.

Gem Sofianos-Boorman, 39, said her experience shows how important the screening is.

She was diagnosed with cervical cancer at 28, following screening, and says it was the last thing she expected, given she was young, healthy and had no symptoms.

She had surgery to remove the cancerous cells plus lymph nodes from her abdomen and pelvis to stop it spreading.

"Looking back, I truly believe that going to my screening appointment saved my life. My cancer was found early, which allowed me to have treatment before it spread.

"That's why it's great news that the NHS is making it more accessible for some people to take part in screening."

Cervical cancer often doesn't cause any symptoms until the disease is more advanced and harder to treat.

"If you receive an invite to cervical screening, or an offer of a self-testing kit, please don't ignore it - it could save your life."

Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women's health, said: "Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game-changer â making it easier than ever for them to get tested.

"There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening â embarrassment, lack of time or worries about discomfort â and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test."

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "Cervical cancer is preventable - but that's why we want to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening."

The kits contain a swab, similar to a long cotton, bud which is used to collect a sample from the vagina.

It is then sent back to the NHS and if high-risk HPV is found, individuals will be invited to book a follow-up cervical screening appointment.

High-risk HPV increases the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not mean a woman will automatically develop it.

Trials of the self-testing in London suggest it could lead to one in 10 women to come forward for screening â boosting uptake by around 400,000 a year.

Other parts of the UK are also looking at introducing self-testing.

Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years â or more frequently if HPV is detected.

Through a combination of HPV vaccination, which is offered to teenagers, and improved screening, the NHS is hoping to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.

The NHS says cervical screening appointments with a clinician is still the best way to prevent cancer â and even if you have missed an appointment you can still come forward for one.

articles.title: Arizona grandpa to undergo amputation after collapsing on scorching sidewalk
articles.summary: A 72-year-old man collapsed on a 120-degree sidewalk in Arizona and suffered severe burns that will require above-knee amputation of his leg.
articles.body: An Arizona grandfather is preparing to undergo an above-knee amputation of his right leg after he tripped and fell while walking outside in Bullhead City during 120-degree heat earlier this month, according to his family. Grant Siler, 72, fell during a walk on Aug. 3 in Bullhead City, causing his body temperature to rise to more than 105 degrees. The family’s GoFundMe said Siler was on the ground for an estimated at least an hour before a passerby found him. The fundraiser said he suffered second and third-degree burns in multiple areas of his body, heat stroke and multiple organ shock. HIKERS FACE URGENT GRAND CANYON HEAT WARNING AFTER TEEN’S DEATH ON POPULAR TRAIL He was then taken to a burn ICU in Las Vegas, where he has been cared for since the incident. When he arrived at the facility, doctors discovered he was suffering from heat stroke and organ shock. "He is in constant pain, can barely move, and has undergone two debridements. Also, he will soon need to undergo surgery for amputation, the extent is not yet known," the GoFundMe reads. During surgery, a surgeon found that tissue in Siler’s right leg was so severely damaged it was unlikely to fully heal, according to an update posted to the fundraiser. Siler is scheduled to have his right leg amputated above the knee on Aug. 31, according to FOX 10 Phoenix. ESPN ANALYST MATT MILLER SAYS HE UNDERWENT LIFE-SAVING AMPUTATION OF LEFT ARM AFTER CAR ACCIDENT "The plan now is to have an above-knee amputation. The Dr's feel he will overall heal faster and have better pain control this way," the fundraiser reads. "We can all imagine that after any amputation, the road to recovery is long and hard...physically, mentally and emotionally," it continued. His wife, Vicki, has been traveling one-and-a-half-hours each way to be with her husband as she continuing to work to support the family’s financial obligations. The family said the couple will also soon have to face medical bills to help with Siler’s recovery. The family is accepting donations to help with home renovations, home medical supplies, prosthetics and other added costs. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Siler's daughter, Heather Crook, recalled an incident in which he dropped an 80-pound cinderblock on his foot but did not even take a Tylenol. "He's hurting really bad," Crook told FOX 10. "He's the 'get up and walk it off' type." "So for him to holler out in pain … it’s really hard to hear. That’s not the kind of person that he is," she added.

articles.title: GLP-1 boom could reshape restaurant bars as diners cut back on alcohol
articles.summary: A new report reveals a growing interest in drink choices among restaurant customers. The report found that health is already influencing some Americans' decisions about alcohol.
articles.body: The rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could be changing more than what Americans put on their plates, as restaurants increasingly look to wellness drinks and other alternatives to traditional alcoholic beverages. The National Restaurant Association's new 2026 Restaurant Beverage Trends report found growing interest in a wider range of drink choices, particularly among younger consumers, as restaurants experiment with everything from wellness and energy drinks to smoothies, lemonades and alcohol-free cocktails. Chad Moutray, chief economist at the Washington, D.C.-based National Restaurant Association, told Fox News Digital that the growing use of GLP-1 medications is one of several health trends restaurant operators are watching. MOVER OVER, APEROL: VIRAL ITALIAN SPRITZ ARRIVES IN US WITH EYE-CATCHING TWIST The report, which was conducted by the National Restaurant Association and is based on surveys of consumers and restaurant operators across the country, found that health is already influencing some Americans' decisions about alcohol. Among adults surveyed who said they don't drink alcohol, 25% cited health reasons. That figure climbed to 34% among Gen Z nondrinkers. Several trends are converging as younger consumers become more health-conscious and GLP-1 medications become more widely used, Moutray said. "I think you're seeing a lot younger folks who are, in general, wanting to be healthier. You have the Make America Healthy Again movement, which is also driving some of this trend," he said. PROTEIN COFFEE IS EXPLODING IN POPULARITY AMONG ADULTS WORRIED ABOUT MUSCLE LOSS "You have people drinking energy drinks and health drinks and all those things. And then you add to that the GLP-1 notion, where if you're taking one of those drugs and your appetite is more suppressed, you're not going to drink as much alcohol." Restaurants are already preparing to broaden their drink selections. Among limited-service restaurant operators, 24% said they planned to add new wellness drinks in 2026, while 26% planned to add energy drinks, 29% smoothies and 27% lemonades. Just under half, 46%, planned to add new coffee offerings. "I think as GLP-1s become less expensive as this year goes on and as we move into 2027, you're going to see restaurant operators continuing to look for alternatives that can be good menu options for consumers that might be taking those drugs," Moutray said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Derek Brown, a hospitality consultant and founder of Drink Company, said he's also seeing GLP-1s contribute to a broader shift toward moderation. "Yeah, there's no doubt that GLP-1s are having an effect on the way that people consume," Brown told Fox News Digital. "And it's part of a basket of things that's contributing to people moderating more often." The drugs can affect people's appetites for both food and drinks, Brown said, potentially leading some customers to consume less alcohol or choose nonalcoholic alternatives. "I think that's clearly part of this entire moderation trend that we're seeing that's just a part of it, but it's significant enough, so I think that's certainly a real thing," Brown said. "And I definitely think that bars and restaurants are starting to feel that." The changing beverage landscape, however, doesn't necessarily mean younger Americans are abandoning alcohol. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Per the report, 71% of Gen Z adults and 74% of millennials surveyed said they drink alcohol either at home or at restaurants. Sixty percent of Gen Z adults and 68% of millennials said they drink alcohol at restaurants. Moutray believes younger consumers are instead choosing from a broader portfolio of drinks. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ That broader selection could be increasingly important for restaurants. The report found that 87% of full-service operators and 80% of limited-service operators said beverages can be an important driver of customer traffic. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's driving traffic, it's getting people excited and it's, hopefully, also helping to improve overall profit margins," Moutray said.

articles.title: Major brain changes that occur around age 50 could impact dementia risk
articles.summary: Microglia decline after age 50 as inflammatory blood-derived immune cells infiltrate the hippocampus, potentially driving neuroinflammation and dementia.
articles.body: The brain may undergo a notable shift at midlife, as new research suggests that its protective immune cells begin to decline and are increasingly replaced by inflammatory cells at around age 50. Researchers from the University of California, San Diego; New York Genome Center; and University of California, Irvine, found that these brain changes may help explain why aging increases the chances of neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, including dementia. The study analyzed postmortem tissue from the hippocampus – the portion of the brain that is responsible for learning and memory – in 40 neurologically healthy adults, ranging from 20 to 95 years of age. THE 'AGE' OF YOUR BLOOD COULD PREDICT DEMENTIA RISK, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS "The most striking change was that after about age 50, the brain’s resident immune cells, called microglia, appear to be increasingly replaced by immune cells that enter from the bloodstream," first author Nathan Zemke, Ph.D., principal investigator at the UC San Diego Center for Epigenomics, told Fox News Digital. "Microglia normally protect the brain by clearing debris and responding to injury, but the incoming cells carry stronger inflammatory signals." The researchers believe this shift may contribute to chronic inflammation linked to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s. They also noted the deterioration of cells involved in maintaining the blood-brain barrier – the protective filter that helps keep harmful substances out of the brain – as well as widespread changes in DNA and gene activity. 'LONGEVITY GENE' MAY PROTECT THE BRAIN FROM ALZHEIMER'S BY BOOSTING DNA REPAIR, STUDY FINDS One of the most exciting implications of the study, according to Zemke, is that the replacement immune cells originate in the blood, which means they are more accessible than cells already deep inside the brain. "It may eventually be possible to modify blood-derived immune cells so that they are more protective and less inflammatory when in the brain," he said. "That could provide an entirely new way to approach Alzheimer’s and other neurological diseases without having to directly manipulate cells within the central nervous system." Although these findings are still in early stages, Zemke said, gaining a better understanding of why this immune-cell replacement happens – and why it happens earlier in some people than others – could lead to new strategies for preserving brain health during aging. The study’s chief limitation is that it studied human brain tissue collected postmortem from different individuals across the adult lifespan, the researchers noted. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "That allows us to identify strong age-related patterns, but it cannot directly show how the same person’s brain changes over decades or prove that a particular cellular change causes cognitive decline or Alzheimer’s disease," Zemke said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "We also do not yet know what triggers the influx of blood-derived immune cells into the brain. Determining whether changes in the blood-brain barrier, inflammation, genetics, lifestyle or other factors initiate this process will be an important next step." The researcher emphasized, however, that he would not recommend that people make any specific medical or lifestyle changes based on this study alone.  "These findings are primarily about understanding the biology of brain aging and identifying new directions for prevention and treatment," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The timing and extent of the brain changes varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that brain aging is not necessarily a fixed process that happens identically in everyone. "The next challenge is to understand what drives that variation and whether some of those factors can be modified," Zemke added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The study also included a small sample of just 40 people and examined tissue only from the hippocampus, meaning the findings may not reflect immune changes throughout the entire brain. The study, which was funded by the National Institutes of Health, was published in the journal Science.

articles.title: 1 in 4 NFL players who died from 2016 to 2021 had CTE, study finds
articles.summary: The study also found dementia was common among brain donors, with researchers urging prevention measures across all levels of the sport.
articles.body: At least 1 in 4 former NFL players who died from 2016 to 2021 was found to have had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), according to a study released on Tuesday. Out of the 878 former players who died during that time frame, 235 donated their brains, researchers said, with 215 of those donated brains found to have CTE, a degenerative disease that can only definitively be diagnosed after death. An NFL spokesperson said: “The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts. “The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust — and expanding — set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well-being. “We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health.” The study’s lead author, Daniel Daneshvar, the chair of physical medicine and rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said that repeated traumatic brain injuries are a known factor in elevated rates of neurodegenerative disease. “Similarly, we and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population,” he added. The study from Mass General Brigham, Boston University and the Concussion & CTE Foundation also found dementia was common among brain donors, with researchers urging prevention measures that focus on cutting down on repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport. “The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn’t occur at the NFL level. They occurred at the collegiate level ... and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level. And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk,” said Daneshvar. The NFL’s 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement limited the number of contact practices during the season. The Ivy League banned full-contact tackling during practices five years later. Out of the 878 former players who died during that time frame, 235 donated their brains, researchers said, with 215 of those donated brains found to have CTE, a degenerative disease that can only definitively be diagnosed after death. An NFL spokesperson said: “The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts. “The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust — and expanding — set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well-being. “We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health.” The study’s lead author, Daniel Daneshvar, the chair of physical medicine and rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said that repeated traumatic brain injuries are a known factor in elevated rates of neurodegenerative disease. “Similarly, we and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population,” he added. articles.title: Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania outbreak, health officials say
articles.summary: They are the first measles-related deaths in the U.S. this year.
articles.body: Two unvaccinated people have died of measles in Pennsylvania’s Lancaster County, the state’s health department confirmed Tuesday. Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen declined to give any additional information about the deaths during a media briefing, citing patient confidentiality. They are the first measles-related deaths in the U.S. this year and the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years. Lancaster County has seen the majority of measles cases in the state’s growing outbreak. As of Tuesday, 393 cases have been confirmed in the state; 86 of them were diagnosed in the past week. So far, 70 people have been hospitalized in Pennsylvania for measles complications. “These tragic deaths remind us that measles is not a harmless illness,” Dr. Jeffrey Martin, a physician at Penn Medicine Lancaster General Hospital, said during the briefing, which was held at Lancaster General Health’s Women & Babies Hospital. “It’s appropriate that we’re having this press conference at our Women & Babies Hospital. Pregnant women and children are vulnerable to measles if they are not vaccinated,” he said. Officials declined to answer a question about whether the deaths involved either a pregnant woman or a baby. Earlier this month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order meant to drive down the number of vaccines recommended for children. The move, which was backed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., drew sharp criticism from pediatricians and public health experts. Kennedy has a history of anti-vaccine rhetoric and, according to local reporting in 2021, was a keynote speaker at an event in Lancaster County in which he said, without citing scientific evidence, that vaccines are harmful. During Tuesday’s media briefing, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said Kennedy had called him to offer resources to assist in the outbreak response. Shapiro said he declined the offer. “I was very, very blunt with him, and I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said. “There’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents.” In a statement, HHS and the CDC expressed condolences to the families and communities affected by the measles deaths. “CDC is working closely with state and local health departments to strengthen response efforts, rapidly support affected communities across the state, and communicate the steps people can take to slow the spread of measles,” the statement said. The grim news comes at a time when more parents than ever are actively avoiding vaccines for their children. During the 2025-26 school year, 4.2% of kindergartners, about 155,000 kids, had at least one vaccine exemption, up from 3.6% the previous school year, according to recent data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The number of kids getting the MMR vaccine in Lancaster County, too, has been falling steadily, from 95.5% in 2017 to 87.6% in 2025. According to the CDC, 2,777 measles cases have been reported nationwide this year, the highest number in 35 years. As of Aug. 20, 193 people with measles, about 7% of cases, had been hospitalized this year. The majority of infected people are unvaccinated. More than 900 measles cases have been counted in the U.S. since May, with Pennsylvania accounting for more than a third of those new cases. Three people died of measles last year: an adult in New Mexico and two young girls in Texas. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, given in two doses around age 1 and age 5, offers 97% protection against measles, usually for life. Children as young as 6 months are eligible for an early, extra dose of the MMR vaccine during outbreaks. “When enough eligible individuals receive the vaccine, the entire community develops a level of immunity that protects our most vulnerable, including babies who are too young to be vaccinated,” Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, wrote in a statement. “I encourage all parents and caregivers to talk with your pediatrician and ask if your child is up-to-date on their MMR vaccine.”

articles.title: Muere Dolly Parton, la reina del country, a los 80 años
articles.summary: Su sobrino ha anunciado la noticia en un comunicado que ha dado pie a cientos de mensajes de compañeros y admiradores
articles.body:
La música no volverá a ser nunca igual sin Dolly Parton, icono intergeneracional que ha puesto la banda sonora a miles de historias. La voz de la reina del country se ha apagado para siempre a los 80 años tras una enfermedad que nunca le quitó las ganas de seguir adelante. Su problema de salud tampoco minimizó su entrega absoluta por una profesión que se ha quedado huérfana con su inesperada muerte. Ha sido su sobrino quien ha confirmado la triste noticia en un comunicado que ha causado una gran conmoción ya que hace solo unos días la propia cantante se pronunció públicamente acerca de su estado y sus planes de futuro.

"Mi nombre es Brin Seaver, hijo de Cassie Parton, y hoy represento a las familias Parton y Owens para anunciar el fallecimiento de mi tía, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, hermana, sobrina y abuela de una generación y Gigi de la siguiente. Este anuncio en video es algo que Dolly me pidió hace años, antes de que lo asimilara por completo como una realidad futura. Como su jefe de seguridad durante más de dos décadas, un cargo que mi padre, Larry, desempeñó antes que yo, había imaginado la gravedad de este momento, pero no la había sentido realmente hasta ahora", ha dicho en un anuncio cuya repercusión ha sido máxima en escasos segundos. Se ha desatado una oleda de mensajes de compañeros que se quedan huérfanos sin ella.

Los detalles de su funeral y el testimonio de su círculo íntimo

La familia de Dolly Parton ha avanzado cómo va a ser la despedida de la artista. Siguiendo sus propios deseos, harán "un pequeño servicio fúnebre privado para los más cercanos" . Animan a todos los admiradores y amigos de la intérprete de 9 to 5 a rendirle homenaje en las redes sociales etiquetando su cuenta o dejando un mensaje en su web oficial. Además, piden que no se compren flores para ella y que ese dinero lo donen a la Imagination Library, iniciativa creada por la propia cantante para fomentar la lectura.

También le han dedicado unas emotivas palabras en las que la definen como una mujer "con una vida llena de brillo que resplandeció con tanta intensidad que todo el mundo pudo verla". "Dolly seguirá siendo para siempre una fuente de inspiración, no solo por su música atemporal y su prolífica carrera como compositora, sino también por su ingenio, calidez y amabilidad, que nos hacían sentir a todos como una familia. El legado de Dolly Parton es de amor, compasión y resiliencia", han añadido. También han remarcado que durante las siete décadas en las que se extendió su carrera "inspiró a múltiples generaciones de artistas y seguidores con su música y su compromiso inquebrantable por hacer del mundo un lugar mejor". Sus canciones, sostienen, seguirán resonando en personas de todas las edades, y su labor filantrópica tendrá un impacto duradero.

La última aparición de Dolly Parton cuatro días antes de su muerte

En medio de la preocupación por la cancelación de los conciertos que tenía previstos para diciembre, la ganadora de 10 premios Grammy tomaba la palabra para hablar en primera persona de su situación. Fue el pasado 21 de agosto cuando se dirigió a sus fans, repartidos por todos los rincones del planeta, para contarles mediante People que estaba lidiando con algunos problemas de salud a los que no les prestó atención cuando cuidaba de su marido. Recordaba que no era la primera vez que se enfrentaba a una situación así porque a principios de los 80 tuvo problemas ginecológicos y de peso.

A pesar de haber atravesado otros episodios complejos, quiso dar su propia versión de los hechos consciente de que ahora la realidad que nos rodea es otra ya que todo es magnifica por el impacto de las redes sociales. "Solía bromear diciendo que era la reina de los tabloides, ¡pero ahora supongo que puedo decir que soy la reina de la IA en las redes sociales! Hablando en serio, aunque todavía me estoy recuperando, ¡sigo trabajando! Ya me conocen, como he dicho muchas veces, me he obsesionado con mis sueños y aún tengo muchas cosas que quiero lograr, así que voy a seguir trabajando todo el tiempo que pueda para verlas hacerse realidad" , aseguraba.

El gran mazazo que la cantante no pudo superar

La vida de Dolly Parton se paró para siempre en marzo de 2025 con la muerte de su gran amor . Carl Thomas Dean fue su compañero incondicional durante 60 años en los que siempre se mantuvo en un segundo plano. No la acompañó a actos públicos porque se sentía cómodo en la sombra, una posición desde la que aportaba calma, serenidad, un apoyo firme y normalidad a su mujer. Ella era una estrella internacional gracias a su talento y su voz, pero en ese brillo que desprendía también tenía un papel fundamental su marido, al que conoció de manera fortuita al salir de una lavandería.

Carl fue además un fuente de inspiración para la artista y así se refleja en canciones como Jolene , una de las más emblemáticas de su extensa discografía. Dolly, que renovó en 2016 los votos matrimoniales con su esposo, siempre compartió con naturalidad el secreto de su unión inquebrantable. "Siempre bromeo y me río cuando la gente me pregunta eso. Nuestra vida es sencilla, pero fácil. Ni siquiera nos hacemos tanta compañía. Viajo mucho, pero realmente disfrutamos el uno del otro cuando estamos juntos y de las pequeñas cosas ". Entre los planes sencillos de los que disfrutaban, viajes en su autocaravana o picnics cerca de casa.

La historia de Dolly Parton, una estrella hecha a sí misma

Ha batido récords en la música vendiendo 160 millones de discos, una cifra aún más increíble si se tiene en cuenta su historia. Dolly Parton nació en 1946 en Pittman Center, Tennessee, en el seno de una familia humilde y muy numerosa, rodeada por once hermanos. Tenía solo seis años cuando se adentró en la música mediante la iglesia, donde cantaba y tocaba la guitarra sin imaginar todo lo que estaba por venir. En 1964 se mudó a Nashville, donde se ganaba la vida tocando en locales. Fue así como llegó su primera gran oportunidad al ser contratada por Porter Wagoner para formar juntos dueto en el programa de televisión The Porter Wagoner Show.

En los 70, cuando ya había definido su característico look con melena rubia y ropa sensual, despegó como un fenómeno internacional al colocarse en el primer puesto de las listas country. Además, fue en esa década cuando compuso la canción que lo cambió todo: I Will Always Love You , un tema que popularizó Whitney Houston en El guardaespalda s, película que protagonizó con Kevin Costner . Y aquello a la vez le abrió las puertas del séptimo arte, en el que ha trabajado como actriz y cantante. Incluso ha ganado un Oscar honorífico y un Emmy, además de ser incluida en el Salón de la Fama de la música country.

Su parte más desconocida, junto a su trayectoria musical, quedaron plasmadas en Dolly Parton, Songteller: My Life in Lyrics. Además, su vida se llevó a las tablas con el montaje Dolly: A True Original Musical, que se estrenó el pasado verano y se estaba moviendo para llevarlo a Broadway a lo largo de este año 2026 . Porque la artista era mucho más que una voz. Destacaba también por su solidaridad, su apoyo a diferentes causas filantrópicas y su ayuda a compañeras más jóvenes como Miley Cyrus, a la que amadrinó profesionalmente. Hoy todas lloran su irreparable pérdida y escuchan en bucle su voz eterna.

articles.title: Michigan Democrat awkwardly pivots to circumcision during heated Fox News debate on child sex changes
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed deflected questions on sex changes for minors, comparing the issue to circumcision.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed addressed questions about sex changes for minors and transgender athletes in women’s sports during a tense exchange on Fox News Monday night. Speaking on "Jesse Watters Primetime," the progressive candidate and former Detroit Health Department director initially avoided giving direct answers on the issues. "Sex changes for minors. Do you support that?" asked host Jesse Watters Monday. HHS OFFICIAL WARNS OF IRREVERSIBLE RISKS AS TRUMP ADMIN RESTRICTS FUNDING FOR YOUTH GENDER PROCEDURES El-Sayed referenced "great conversations" about right-to-try legislation and said he believes the government should not limit the healthcare a person is allowed to receive. "I just think the government shouldn't tell you what kind of healthcare you should have and if you're a minor, it's between you and your doctor and your parents," El-Sayed said. FTC ALLEGES INFLUENTIAL TRANSGENDER HEALTH ORGANIZATION MISLED PARENTS ABOUT SAFETY OF YOUTH TREATMENTS "If you disagree that healthcare decisions need to be made by a doctor, their parents and a patient, then I just think we agree to disagree. But you know, you want to put government inside a clinic or a hospital selectively," he added. Watters then asked El-Sayed if he supported cutting off the genitalia of minors. El-Sayed responded by raising circumcision as another example involving parental consent in medical care for children, asking Watters if he himself is circumcised. "I mean, so do you really want to have this conversation? Are you circumcised?" El-Sayed asked. "I think it’s a problem that you think that you get to decide what happens between a parent, a doctor and a patient. And I'm just saying that, yes, circumcision is surgery on a kid's ding-a-ling. So if you really want to bring that up, you can. I just think you guys are really selective about how you want to talk about these things," he later added. ABDUL EL-SAYED’S MEDICARE-FOR-ALL CRUSADE COLLIDES WITH AN AWKWARD CONTRADICTION INVOLVING HIS WIFE "Abdul, Michigan's not going for that. That is sick stuff," Watters responded before moving the conversation toward transgender athletes in women’s sports. El-Sayed initially declined to answer the question, instead saying Watters had not asked about issues "people actually care about in Michigan," including groceries and healthcare. articles.title: Deadly measles outbreak hits Northeast as state records first deaths in 35 years
articles.summary: Two unvaccinated Lancaster County residents died from measles, marking Pennsylvania's first measles deaths in 35 years amid 393 confirmed cases.
articles.body: Pennsylvania confirmed two measles-related deaths on Tuesday, according to the state’s department of health. This marks the first losses related to the highly contagious virus within the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in 35 years. The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed that both Lancaster County individuals were unvaccinated, noting that the best way to prevent measles infection is to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL The MMR vaccine administered over two doses can boost a person’s immune system and provide 97% lifetime protection, according to health officials. In a press release, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen shared her "deepest sympathies" with the "loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss." "Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness," she said in the statement. "We want to ensure that every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles." The state's DOH has confirmed 393 cases of measles in 28 counties so far in 2026. Measles is a highly contagious virus that can be fatal in one to three patients per 1,000 cases, data shows. The virus can cause long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Nearly 20% of individuals who contract measles are hospitalized. Measles spreads when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, spreading the virus through respiratory droplets. It can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the person leaves the area, experts caution. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Early measles symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A measles rash follows a few days later, starting on the head and spreading down to the rest of the body. Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. Those who believe they were exposed to measles should contact a healthcare provider. Dr. Jesse Goodman, former FDA chief scientist in Washington, D.C., spoke with Fox News Digital about the MMR vaccine, calling it "extremely safe and highly effective." "The vaccine prevents millions of measles deaths worldwide annually, including hundreds that used to occur in the U.S.," he said. "There is no evidence that MMR vaccine causes any chronic illnesses, including autism." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Dr. Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, Maryland, agreed that Pennsylvania's 35-year streak without a measles-related death "wasn't luck." "It was the vaccine working so completely that an entire generation of parents grew up never seeing what this virus does to a child’s lungs or brain," he told Fox News Digital. "That protection is increasingly not valued, and this is the predictable result when the population turns their back on a life-saving technology." Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, previously emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles amid elevated case counts across the U.S. "Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, stressing the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel. "In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn’t about personal choice, it’s about community protection. We need to protect those who can’t have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant."

articles.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
articles.summary: They work better than patches, gum or pills, the most up-to-date evidence suggests.
articles.body:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine , external , which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

Experts say vaping, although not entirely risk-free, is far safer than smoking.

In the UK, there are now more over-16s using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, figures show . Around 5.3 million people or 10% of adults say they smoke, while around 5.4 million use vapes daily or occasionally.

The review , external of the most recent and best quality evidence to date applies to regulated vapes that are checked for quality and compliant with strict safety laws.

It doesn't look at unregulated ones that can contain illicit substances, like spice or THC.

One of the report authors, Dr Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, cautioned: "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals.

"Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body."

The review found no evidence of any increased risk of serious harm from using e-cigarettes to quit.

The long-term risks of vaping are not yet clear though, and the NHS says children and non-smokers should never vape.

Doctors say vaping could lead to health harms in children and should be made "less attractive" to them.

Around two in three people who smoke long-term will die from a tobacco-related illness, says the charity Action on Smoking and Health.

According to the World Health Organization, smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million people a year.

Quitting smoking reduces your risk of serious illnesses like heart disease, lung cancer, and stroke.

Almost every local NHS stop smoking service provides vapes or other support to help people quit.

You can search online , external for your local service with your postcode.
